name: Bagan
info: Bagan, formerly Pagan, is the medieval capital of the Pagan Kingdom on the Irrawaddy in Myanmar, where rulers and their subjects raised thousands of Buddhist temples, pagodas and monasteries between the 11th and 13th centuries, over 2,300 of which survive.

facts.made: The rulers of the Pagan Kingdom and their wealthy subjects, with brickmakers, masons, metalworkers, carpenters, woodcarvers and potters; the city was founded by the Mranma (Burmans) according to Western scholarship
facts.form: A walled core, Old Bagan (140 hectares), within a strip of monuments about 9 km long on the east bank of the Irrawaddy, spread over an archaeological zone of 13 km by 8 km; stupa-style solid temples and gu-style hollow temples
facts.where: The Mandalay Region of Myanmar, on the bend of the Irrawaddy, 290 km south-west of Mandalay and 700 km north of Yangon; finds are kept in the Bagan Archaeological Museum
facts.known: the remains of over 2,300 temples and pagodas; the stupas and the gu-style hollow temples; vaulting techniques developed at Bagan; the pentagonal temple plan; the Myazedi inscriptions; the Konbaung-period and 1990s restorations; inscription as a World Heritage Site in 2019

t: From 1044 to 1287 Bagan was the capital and the political, economic and cultural centre of the Pagan Empire, and its rulers and wealthy subjects built over 10,000 religious monuments in an area of 104 km2.

Building peaked between about 1150 and 1200, when most of the largest monuments went up; the earliest vaulted temples date to the 11th century, and the vaulting seems to have developed at Bagan itself.

Bagan outlived its empire as a settlement and a pilgrimage place, but earthquakes damaged it badly in 1975 and 2016, and its restorations of the 1990s were widely condemned before it was listed by UNESCO in 2019.
dyk: The vaulting techniques of the Bagan era were lost in later periods: in the 18th century King Bodawpaya tried to build the Mingun Pagoda as a spacious vaulted temple but failed, as the craftsmen and masons of his time had lost the knowledge of vaulting and keystone arching.
ev: According to the Burmese chronicles, King Pyinbya fortified Bagan, while Western scholarship holds that the Mranma founded it in the mid-to-late 9th century
Bagan became the capital and the political, economic and cultural centre of the Bagan Empire, a position it held until 1287
The peak of monument building began; it lasted until about 1200 and produced most of the largest buildings
The Pagan Empire collapsed, which the chronicles attribute to repeated Mongol invasions between 1277 and 1301
Bagan formally ceased to be the capital when the Myinsaing Kingdom became the new power in Upper Burma
The Konbaung period began; its state-sponsored renovations, which lasted until 1885, were mostly not true to the original designs
A major earthquake on 8 July damaged many temples, some of them irreparably
UNESCO inscribed Bagan as a World Heritage Site, 24 years after its first nomination

sections.origins:
According to the Burmese chronicles, Bagan was founded in the second century CE and fortified in 849 by King Pyinbya, the 34th successor of the founder of early Bagan. Western scholarship holds instead that it was founded in the mid-to-late 9th century by the Mranma (Burmans), who had recently entered the Irrawaddy valley from the Nanzhao Kingdom. It was one of several competing Pyu city-states until the late 10th century, when the Burman settlement grew in authority and grandeur. Its classical Pali name was Arimaddanapura, "the City that Tramples on Enemies".

From 1044 to 1287 Bagan was the capital and the political, economic and cultural centre of the Bagan Empire. Its religion was fluid and syncretic, largely a continuation of the Pyu era, in which Theravada Buddhism lived beside Mahayana and Tantric Buddhism, Hindu Saivite and Vaishnava schools and native nat traditions. Royal patronage of Theravada Buddhism since the mid-11th century let that school gradually gain primacy, while the others continued to thrive throughout the Pagan period.
sections.content:
The Bagan Archaeological Zone covers an area of 13 km by 8 km on the bend of the Irrawaddy, 290 km south-west of Mandalay. A main strip about 9 km long extends along the east bank of the river, with the walled core known as Old Bagan in the middle. The core, of 140 hectares, is surrounded by three walls; a fourth, on the western side, may once have existed before the river washed it away. Old Bagan takes up only a small part of the 8,000-hectare area where monuments are found, which suggests that it represented an elite core and not an urban boundary.

The temples fall into two broad categories. The stupa, also called a pagoda or chedi, is a solid structure, typically with a relic chamber inside. The gu-style temple is a hollow structure used for meditation, devotional worship of the Buddha and other Buddhist rituals, built in a one-face design, with one main entrance, or a four-face design, with four. Pairs or series of ogres as guardian figures, called bilu, were a favourite theme in the decoration of stupas, and a gallery of terracotta tiles depicting jataka stories often ran round the terraces of a pagoda.
sections.making:
Over about 250 years Bagan's rulers and their wealthy subjects built over 10,000 religious monuments, approximately 1,000 stupas, 10,000 small temples and 3,000 monasteries, in an area of 104 km2. The basic layout had taken shape by the late 11th century, the first major period of building, and construction then appears to have been relatively decentralised, possibly at the village level. The peak came between about 1150 and 1200, when most of the largest buildings were built and the most building material was used. In the 13th century more monasteries and smaller monuments were built, which Michael Aung-Thwin reads as a sign of dwindling economic resources and growing monastic influence.

Bagan stupas evolved from Pyu designs, which were based on stupas of the Andhra region of south-eastern India and, to a smaller extent, of Ceylon. By the 11th century the stupa had become more bell-shaped, and the Shwezigon and Shwesandaw Pagodas are the earliest examples. The techniques of vaulting seem to have developed at Bagan itself, the earliest vaulted temples dating to the 11th century. The pentagonal plan also originated there, to include veneration of the Maitreya Buddha. The work employed brickmakers, masons, metalworkers, carpenters, woodcarvers and potters, who were paid well.
sections.reception:
Bagan became a cosmopolitan centre of religious and secular studies, specialising in Pali scholarship in grammar and abhidhamma, the philosophical-psychological studies of Buddhism, with works in a variety of languages on prosody, phonology, astrology, alchemy, medicine and legal studies. It attracted monks and students from as far as India, Sri Lanka and the Khmer Empire. Contemporary inscriptions indicate that people of many linguistic and cultural backgrounds lived and worked there, and the city, once home to some 50,000 to 200,000 people, drew immigrants from regions then in decline, such as Dvaravati, Srivijaya and the Chola Empire.

After the empire fell, Bagan survived into the 15th century as a settlement and remained a pilgrimage destination, but pilgrimage focused on "a score or so" of the most prominent temples, among them the Ananda, the Shwezigon, the Sulamani, the Htilominlo and the Dhammayazika. Devotees repainted many temples with new frescoes over the Pagan-era ones or fitted them with new Buddha statues. Fewer than 200 temples were built between the 15th and 20th centuries.
sections.survival:
The Pagan Empire collapsed in 1287, which the Burmese chronicles attribute to repeated Mongol invasions. Recent research shows that Mongol armies may not have reached Bagan, and that if they did, the damage was probably minimal. Michael Aung-Thwin suggests instead that the provincial governors who defended against the Mongols became the new power elite, so that their capitals became the political centres and Bagan a backwater. The thousands of less famous temples fell into disrepair, and most did not survive. Systematic renovations in the Konbaung period (1752-1885) were largely not true to the original designs, and the interiors of some temples, such as the Thatbyinnyu and the Ananda, were whitewashed.

Bagan lies in an active earthquake zone, with over 400 recorded earthquakes between 1904 and 1975. The quake of 8 July 1975 damaged many temples, severely and irreparably in cases such as the Bupaya. A major earthquake on 24 August 2016 caused major damage to nearly 400 temples, and visitors were prohibited from 33 much-damaged ones. The Zamani Project documented 12 monuments with LiDAR between 2017 and 2018.
sections.legacy:
Bagan's stupas were the prototypes for later Burmese stupas in symbolism, form, design, building techniques and even materials. The masonry of its buildings shows "an astonishing degree of perfection", and many of the immense structures survived the 1975 earthquake more or less intact. Its vaulting was not matched afterwards: only much smaller gu-style temples were built after Bagan.

In the 1990s the military government restored many damaged pagodas, seeking to make Bagan an international tourist destination. The restorations drew widespread condemnation from art historians and preservationists worldwide, who objected that they paid little attention to original architectural styles and used modern materials; the government also established a golf course, a paved highway and a 61 m watchtower. Bagan was not listed by UNESCO until 6 July 2019, allegedly mainly on account of the restorations, and it became the second World Heritage Site in Myanmar after the Ancient Cities of Pyu. The Bagan Archaeological Museum holds the original Myazedi inscriptions, called the Rosetta Stone of Burma.

summary: Bagan, the capital of the Pagan Kingdom from 1044 to 1287, was the site of over 10,000 Buddhist monuments built mainly between the 11th and 13th centuries. Earthquakes and renovations altered it, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2019.
